lesson.title: The Data Plane: Where Every Packet Actually Moves
lesson.summary: The data plane is the part of a network device that forwards packets according to rules that have already been decided, doing so quickly and repeatedly for every packet, without deciding policy itself.
lesson.body:
Every network device that forwards traffic, a home router, an enterprise switch, a router at the core of the internet, is really doing two different jobs at once. One job is deciding what should happen to a given packet: which interface it should leave from, whether it should be dropped, whether its header should be rewritten. The other job is actually doing that thing, over and over, for every packet that arrives, at whatever speed the physical link allows. The data plane is the second job. It is the part of the device that reads each incoming packet, checks it against a table of forwarding rules that have already been decided, and sends the packet on its way. It does not decide policy. It executes it.

This distinction matters because of forwarding, the basic operation of moving a packet from an incoming interface to the correct outgoing interface based on its destination. Forwarding is what the data plane does, continuously and at high volume. A core internet router might need to make a forwarding decision for hundreds of millions of packets per second. To do that, the data plane typically does not run general purpose software for each packet. Instead it uses specialized hardware, often an ASIC (application specific integrated circuit) built specifically for fast table lookups, so that a decision like this destination IP matches this table entry, send it out port 12, can happen in nanoseconds rather than the milliseconds a general purpose CPU might need.

A concrete example makes this clearer. Picture a router with a forwarding table containing hundreds of thousands of IP prefixes, each pointing to an outgoing interface and a next hop address. When a packet destined for, say, 8.8.8.8 arrives, the data plane performs a longest prefix match against that table, finds the most specific matching entry, rewrites the packet's link layer header as needed, and pushes it out the matching interface. It does this the same way for the next packet, and the packet after that, regardless of what application generated the traffic or what the packet contains. The rules themselves came from somewhere else, typically a routing protocol or, as later chapters explore, a centralized controller, but the data plane does not care where the rules came from. It only cares about applying them fast and consistently.

Separating decide the rule from apply the rule this cleanly is what makes modern networking scale. If every packet required a complex decision process from scratch, networks would be far slower and far less predictable. Keeping the data plane simple and fast, and pushing the harder decisions elsewhere, is a design pattern that reappears throughout this chapter sequence, most directly in OpenFlow and software defined networking, where that elsewhere becomes an explicit, programmable, centralized controller.
